Notes on distributed consensus

Posted 4 March 2026 · 11 min read

Consensus protocols are usually introduced through their safety properties, which is a mistake. Safety is the easy half. What actually determines whether a protocol survives contact with a real network is how it behaves when liveness is threatened — during partitions, clock skew, and the long tail of partial failures that no formal model bothers to enumerate.

Why quorums are not the interesting part

Every textbook treatment spends its first chapter on quorum intersection. The arithmetic is genuinely simple: any two majorities of an odd-sized set must share a member, and that shared member is enough to carry a decision forward. Once you have internalised that, quorums stop being interesting.

What remains interesting is the leader. Almost every practical protocol funnels decisions through one, because doing otherwise costs a round trip, and the difference between one round trip and two is the difference between a system people enjoy using and one they route around.

Failure detectors in practice

A failure detector is a timeout with better marketing. The literature treats detection as an abstract oracle; production systems treat it as a tuning parameter that someone set during an incident three years ago and nobody has dared touch since.

if now() - last_heartbeat > election_timeout {
    become_candidate()
}

The consequence is that the election timeout becomes the single most load-bearing constant in the system. Set it too low and a garbage-collection pause triggers a spurious election. Set it too high and a genuinely dead leader stalls writes for seconds.

What I would tell a past version of myself

  • Measure the tail, not the median. The median is never where consensus systems fail.
  • Log every state transition with a monotonic term number; you will need it at 3am.
  • Treat clock skew as adversarial even inside a single datacenter.
  • Write the partition test before you write the happy path.

Further reading: the Raft paper, and the Jepsen analyses, which remain the only literature that consistently tests what the papers claim.
